newsitem.title: JAPAN: China asks Japan to rase lighthouse on islands.
newsitem.headline: China asks Japan to rase lighthouse on islands.

text.p: China's Vice Foreign Minister Tang Jiaxuan asked Japan on Tuesday to tear down a lighthouse to defuse a row over disputed islands in the East China Sea, a Japanese Foreign Ministry official said.

In a meeting with Japanese Deputy Foreign Minister Shunji Yanai in Tokyo, Tang also said that China was concerned about Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto's visit to a controversial Japanese war shrine, the official said.
"The most important thing is for the Japanese side to take appropriate measures to resolve the issue (over the islands)," he said Tang told Yanai.
"You have done nothing effective to resolve this. We must repeat our demands to remove the lighthouse and ensure a similar thing does not happen in the future," Tang said.

Japan, China and Taiwan are locked in a dispute over a group of tiny uninhabited islands, which Japan calls the Senkakus and China calls the Diaoyus. The row flared up after Japanese ultra-nationalists erected the lighthouse on one of the islands earlier this year.
The meeting of the two vice-ministers was the first formal talks between senior diplomats of Japan and China since their foreign ministers had a brief meeting last month in New York.

Senior Japanese Foreign Ministry officials have said the dispute over the islands, and Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto's visit to a controversial war shrine, have plunged bilateral relations to their worst state since normalisation in 1978.
Tang also told Yanai that actions and remarks by Japanese politicians regarding Japan's record in World War Two could have severe repercussions, the Japanese official said.

"The Chinese people are angered by this (Hashimoto's) visit to the Yasukuni Shrine," Tang told Yanai. "It is important that you make these pledges regarding historical perspectives, but actions are more important than words."

In July, Hashimoto became the first Japanese prime minister in a decade to visit Yasukuni, which symbolically enshrines the spirit of Japan's 2.6 million war dead since the late 19th century. They include World War Two leader General Hideki Tojo.
It has been the islands row, however, which has been the biggest recent irritant in relations.
Japanese coastguard vessels have tried to keep Taiwanese and Hong Kong protesters from landing on the islands, but some have gone ashore and waved flags in protest.
